claim: CAGE (Cap Analysis of Gene Expression) was used to profile transcription start sites (TSSs) across 108 Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-transformed lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) of African origin.
source: To characterize human variability in promoter activities, we profiled TSSs using CAGE (Cap Analysis of Gene Expression Takahashi et al., 2012; Figure 1A) across 108 Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-transformed LCLs (Auton et al., 2015) of African origin, 89 from Yoruba in Ibadan, Nigeria (YRI) and 19 from Luhya in Webuye, Kenya (LWK) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the experimental method (CAGE) and sample characteristics (108 EBV-transformed LCLs of African origin).

claim: The LCL panel consisted of 89 samples from Yoruba in Ibadan, Nigeria (YRI) and 19 from Luhya in Webuye, Kenya (LWK).
source: To characterize human variability in promoter activities, we profiled TSSs using CAGE (Cap Analysis of Gene Expression Takahashi et al., 2012; Figure 1A) across 108 Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-transformed LCLs (Auton et al., 2015) of African origin, 89 from Yoruba in Ibadan, Nigeria (YRI) and 19 from Luhya in Webuye, Kenya (LWK) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the population composition of the sample panel.

claim: The LCL panel had a balanced sex ratio with 56 females and 52 males.
source: The samples had a balanced sex ratio, 56 females and 52 males, and no observable population stratification in the expression data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sex distribution of the samples.

claim: No observable population stratification was detected in the expression data.
source: The samples had a balanced sex ratio, 56 females and 52 males, and no observable population stratification in the expression data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing principal component analysis.

claim: 29,001 active promoters of 15,994 annotated genes were identified through positional clustering of proximal CAGE-inferred TSSs.
source: We identified 29,001 active promoters of 15,994 annotated genes (Frankish et al., 2019) through positional clustering of proximal CAGE-inferred TSSs on the same strand (Figure 1A; Carninci et al., 2006) detected in at least 10% of individuals (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of promoters and genes identified using the described clustering method.

claim: Promoters were required to be detected in at least 10% of individuals to be included in the analysis.
source: We identified 29,001 active promoters of 15,994 annotated genes (Frankish et al., 2019) through positional clustering of proximal CAGE-inferred TSSs on the same strand (Figure 1A; Carninci et al., 2006) detected in at least 10% of individuals (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the detection threshold used for promoter identification.

claim: Promoter CV2 (squared coefficient of variation) decreases with increasing mean expression.
source: We observed that the promoter CV2 decreases by increasing mean expression (Figure 1E; Eling et al., 2018; Kolodziejczyk et al., 2015; Sigalova et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this relationship and references Figure 1E showing the data, along with citations to prior work.

claim: The expected dispersion for each promoter was subtracted according to its expression level to adjust for the mean expression-dispersion relationship.
source: To account for this bias, we subtracted the expected dispersion for each promoter according to its expression level (Kolodziejczyk et al., 2015; Newman et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the adjustment method used, with citations to prior methodological work.

claim: Rank differences in promoter dispersion were maintained for each expression level after adjustment.
source: Importantly, rank differences in promoter dispersion were maintained for each expression level after adjustment, as seen for promoters of genes RPL26L1 and SIX3 (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation and references figures showing examples.

claim: A convolutional neural network (CNN) model can distinguish between low variable promoters (N=5,054) and highly variable promoters (N=5,683) based on their local DNA sequence with high accuracy (AUC=0.84).
source: The resulting model was capable of distinguishing between these promoter classes with high accuracy (area under receiving operating curve (AUC)=0.84 for the out of sample test set; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), equally well for highl and low variable promoters (per-class test set F1 scores of 0.76 and 0.77, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the model performance metrics.

claim: The CNN model achieved per-class test set F1 scores of 0.76 and 0.77 for high and low variable promoters, respectively.
source: The resulting model was capable of distinguishing between these promoter classes with high accuracy (area under receiving operating curve (AUC)=0.84 for the out of sample test set; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), equally well for highl and low variable promoters (per-class test set F1 scores of 0.76 and 0.77, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the F1 scores for both promoter classes.

claim: Motifs for the ETS superfamily of transcription factors, including ELK1, ETV6, and ELK3, are associated with low variable promoters.
source: Noteworthy, we observed motifs for the ETS superfamily of TFs, including ELK1, ETV6, and ELK3, associated with low variable promoters, and motifs for PTF1A, ASCL2, and FOS-JUN heterodimer (AP-1) among highly variable promoters.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states which TF motifs are associated with low variable promoters based on DeepLift analysis.

claim: Motifs for PTF1A, ASCL2, and FOS-JUN heterodimer (AP-1) are associated with highly variable promoters.
source: Noteworthy, we observed motifs for the ETS superfamily of TFs, including ELK1, ETV6, and ELK3, associated with low variable promoters, and motifs for PTF1A, ASCL2, and FOS-JUN heterodimer (AP-1) among highly variable promoters.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states which TF motifs are associated with highly variable promoters.

claim: The promoter sequence and its putative TF binding sites are predictive of the expression variability of a promoter.
source: These results demonstrate that the promoter sequence and its putative TF binding sites are predictive of the expression variability of a promoter.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the CNN and motif discovery results.

claim: A random forest classifier based on TF binding site profiles and CpG content achieved an AUC of 0.79 for predicting promoter variability.
source: Feature selection (Kursa and Rudnicki, 2010) identified 124 of the 746 TFs as well as CpG ratio to be important for classification, and a classifier based on these selected features demonstrated high predictive performance (AUC = 0.79; per-class F1 score of 0.73 and 0.68 for low and highly variable promoters, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), reinforcing the strong link observed between DNA sequence and promoter variability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the performance of the random forest model.

claim: 124 of 746 TFs and CpG ratio were identified as important features for classifying promoter variability.
source: Feature selection (Kursa and Rudnicki, 2010) identified 124 of the 746 TFs as well as CpG ratio to be important for classification, and a classifier based on these selected features demonstrated high predictive performance (AUC = 0.79; per-class F1 score of 0.73 and 0.68 for low and highly variable promoters, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), reinforcing the strong link observed between DNA sequence and promoter variability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of features selected by the Boruta method.

claim: High observed/expected CpG ratio is the strongest predictive feature of low promoter variability.
source: We identified the presence of high observed/expected CpG ratio and TATA-binding protein (TBP) binding sites (TATA-boxes) to be the strongest predictive features of low and high promoter variability, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding from the SHAP analysis of the random forest model.

claim: TATA-binding protein (TBP) binding sites (TATA-boxes) are the strongest predictive feature of high promoter variability.
source: We identified the presence of high observed/expected CpG ratio and TATA-binding protein (TBP) binding sites (TATA-boxes) to be the strongest predictive features of low and high promoter variability, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding from the SHAP analysis.

claim: A baseline model based on CpG ratio and TBP binding site presence alone yielded worse performance (AUC = 0.71) than the full model (AUC = 0.79).
source: Although the remaining TFs contribute only marginally on their own to the predictions compared to TATA-box and high CpG content status (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), a baseline model (decision tree) based on CpG ratio and TBP binding site presence alone yielded worse performance than the full model (AUC = 0.71 vs 0.79 for the baseline model and the full model, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the performance of the baseline and full models.

claim: The TF binding grammar contributes to a promoter's expression variability beyond CpG content and TATA-box presence.
source: This demonstrates that the TF binding grammar contributes to a promoter's expression variability.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the comparison of baseline and full models.

claim: TFs associated with highly variable promoters are mostly related to tissue-specific or developmental regulation.
source: TFs associated with highly variable promoters are mostly related to tissue-specific or developmental regulation (e.g., FOXP2, HOXA10) while TFs predictive of low promoter variability are generally associated with ubiquitous activity across cell types and a diverse range of basic cellular processes (e.g. ELK1, ELF4, ETV3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly characterizes the functional associations of TFs predictive of high variability.

claim: TFs predictive of low promoter variability are generally associated with ubiquitous activity across cell types and basic cellular processes.
source: TFs associated with highly variable promoters are mostly related to tissue-specific or developmental regulation (e.g., FOXP2, HOXA10) while TFs predictive of low promoter variability are generally associated with ubiquitous activity across cell types and a diverse range of basic cellular processes (e.g. ELK1, ELF4, ETV3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly characterizes the functional associations of TFs predictive of low variability.

claim: TFs predictive of high variability tend to have binding sites in relatively few highly variable promoters.
source: In addition, TFs predictive of high variability (e.g. ZIC2, ZNF449, HOXA10) tend to have binding sites in relatively few highly variable promoters while TFs predictive of low promoter variability (e.g. ELK1, ELK3) show a propensity for having binding sites present in a large number of promoters (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation based on analysis of TF binding site frequency.

claim: TFs predictive of low promoter variability show a propensity for having binding sites present in a large number of promoters.
source: In addition, TFs predictive of high variability (e.g. ZIC2, ZNF449, HOXA10) tend to have binding sites in relatively few highly variable promoters while TFs predictive of low promoter variability (e.g. ELK1, ELK3) show a propensity for having binding sites present in a large number of promoters (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Variably expressed promoters have diverse TF binding profiles.
source: This suggests that variably expressed promoters have diverse TF binding profiles and that the regulatory grammar for promoter stability is less complex.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation based on the TF binding site analysis.

claim: The regulatory grammar for promoter stability is less complex than that for variably expressed promoters.
source: This suggests that variably expressed promoters have diverse TF binding profiles and that the regulatory grammar for promoter stability is less complex.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: The presence of binding sites for some TFs that are predictive of promoter variability are also associated with promoter expression level.
source: Although the adjusted dispersion of promoters was separated from their expression level (Figure 1E), we observed that the presence of binding sites for some TFs that are predictive of promoter variability are also associated with promoter expression level (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation and references supporting figure.

claim: The effect of identified features on promoter variability is evident across a range of promoter expression levels.
source: Importantly, despite this association, the effect of identified features on promoter variability is still evident across a range of promoter expression levels (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation with reference to supporting figures.

claim: CpG islands have an attenuating effect on promoter variability regardless of expression level.
source: This is particularly apparent for CpG islands, which seem to have an attenuating effect on promoter variability regardless of expression level (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: Many TFs identified as being predictive of low variability belong to the ETS family of transcription factors.
source: Many of the TFs identified as being predictive of low variability (e.g. ELK1, ELK3, ELF4, ETV2, ETV3) belong to the ETS family of TFs (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), a large group of TFs that are conserved across Metazoa and characterized by their shared ETS domain that binds 5′-GGA(A/T)–3′ DNA sequences (Sharrocks, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation and provides citation for ETS family characteristics.

claim: ETS factors are important regulators of promoter activities in lymphoid cells.
source: ETS factors are important regulators of promoter activities in lymphoid cells (Hepkema et al., 2020), but are generally involved in a wide range of crucial cellular processes such as growth, proliferation, apoptosis, and cellular homeostasis (Kar and Gutierrez-Hartmann, 2013; Oikawa and Yamada, 2003; Suico et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this with citation to prior work.

claim: Different ETS factors can bind in a redundant manner to the same promoters of housekeeping genes.
source: Furthermore, different ETS factors can bind in a redundant manner to the same promoters of housekeeping genes (Hollenhorst et al., 2011; Hollenhorst et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this with citations to prior work.

claim: ETS binding site presence is associated with lower variability across all expression levels.
source: Although in general linked with higher promoter activity (Curina et al., 2017), ETS binding site presence is associated with lower variability across all expression levels (Figure 2G).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation with reference to Figure 2G and citation.

claim: The degree of promoter variability decreases with an increasing number of non-overlapping ETS binding sites.
source: In addition, the degree of promoter variability decreases by an increasing number of non-overlapping ETS binding sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A), regardless of promoter expression level (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B), suggesting that multiple ETS binding sites can either facilitate cooperativity between ETS factors or provide robustness to stabilize promoter variability across individuals.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation with references to supporting figures.

claim: Multiple ETS binding sites can either facilitate cooperativity between ETS factors or provide robustness to stabilize promoter variability across individuals.
source: In addition, the degree of promoter variability decreases by an increasing number of non-overlapping ETS binding sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A), regardless of promoter expression level (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B), suggesting that multiple ETS binding sites can either facilitate cooperativity between ETS factors or provide robustness to stabilize promoter variability across individuals.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly suggests these two possible mechanisms based on the data.

claim: Promoter sequence can influence both low and high promoter variability across human individuals independently from its impact on expression level.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that promoter sequence can influence both low and high promoter variability across human individuals independently from its impact on expression level.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the modeling results.

claim: Variable promoters exhibit highly diverse binding grammars for TFs that are associated with relatively few promoters.
source: Our results further indicate that variable promoters exhibit highly diverse binding grammars for TFs that are associated with relatively few promoters, while a more uniform regulatory grammar is indicated for stable promoters, being highly associated with higher CpG content and ETS binding sites.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the TF binding analysis.

claim: A more uniform regulatory grammar is indicated for stable promoters, being highly associated with higher CpG content and ETS binding sites.
source: Our results further indicate that variable promoters exhibit highly diverse binding grammars for TFs that are associated with relatively few promoters, while a more uniform regulatory grammar is indicated for stable promoters, being highly associated with higher CpG content and ETS binding sites.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: Low variable promoters are highly enriched with basic cellular housekeeping processes, in particular metabolic processes.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, we observed that low variable promoters were highly enriched with basic cellular housekeeping processes, in particular metabolic processes (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation from GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: Highly variable promoters are enriched with more dynamic biological functions, including signaling, response to stimulus, and developmental processes.
source: In contrast, highly variable promoters were enriched with more dynamic biological functions, including signaling, response to stimulus, and developmental processes.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation from GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes of highly variable promoters tend to have higher transcriptional noise than those of low variable ones across GM12878 single cells (Cohen's d=0.411, p<2.2 × 10–16).
source: In agreement, genes of highly variable promoters tend to have higher transcriptional noise than those of low variable ones across GM12878 single cells (Cohen's d=0.411, p<2.2 × 10–16, two sample t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation with statistical test results.

claim: There is an inverse correlation between variability in promoter activity and the number of cell types the corresponding gene is expressed in (Spearman's rank correlation ρ = −0.21, p< 2.2 × 10–16).
source: Furthermore, we observed an inverse correlation between variability in promoter activity and the number of cell types (FANTOM Consortium and the RIKEN PMI and CLST (DGT) et al., 2014) and tissues (Battle et al., 2017) the corresponding gene is expressed in (Spearman's rank correlation ρ = −0.21 and −0.15 for cell types and tissues, respectively, p< 2.2 × 10–16; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating that highly variable promoters are more cell-type and tissue specific in their expression.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this correlation with statistical test results.

claim: There is an inverse correlation between variability in promoter activity and the number of tissues the corresponding gene is expressed in (Spearman's rank correlation ρ = −0.15, p< 2.2 × 10–16).
source: Furthermore, we observed an inverse correlation between variability in promoter activity and the number of cell types (FANTOM Consortium and the RIKEN PMI and CLST (DGT) et al., 2014) and tissues (Battle et al., 2017) the corresponding gene is expressed in (Spearman's rank correlation ρ = −0.21 and −0.15 for cell types and tissues, respectively, p< 2.2 × 10–16; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating that highly variable promoters are more cell-type and tissue specific in their expression.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this correlation with statistical test results.

claim: Highly variable promoters are more cell-type and tissue specific in their expression.
source: Furthermore, we observed an inverse correlation between variability in promoter activity and the number of cell types (FANTOM Consortium and the RIKEN PMI and CLST (DGT) et al., 2014) and tissues (Battle et al., 2017) the corresponding gene is expressed in (Spearman's rank correlation ρ = −0.21 and −0.15 for cell types and tissues, respectively, p< 2.2 × 10–16; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating that highly variable promoters are more cell-type and tissue specific in their expression.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the correlation analysis.

claim: Up-regulated promoters after TNFα treatment are enriched among highly variable promoters (odds ratio=1.529, p=4.563 × 10–8).
source: This revealed enrichment of up-regulated promoters among highly variable promoters (odds ratio (OR)=1.529, p=4.563 × 10–8, Fisher's exact test) as posited, while low variable promoters were mostly unaffected or down-regulated (OR = 0.459, p<2.2 × 10–16, Fisher's exact test; Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this enrichment with statistical test results.

claim: Low variable promoters were mostly unaffected or down-regulated after TNFα treatment (odds ratio = 0.459, p<2.2 × 10–16).
source: This revealed enrichment of up-regulated promoters among highly variable promoters (odds ratio (OR)=1.529, p=4.563 × 10–8, Fisher's exact test) as posited, while low variable promoters were mostly unaffected or down-regulated (OR = 0.459, p<2.2 × 10–16, Fisher's exact test; Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation with statistical test results.

claim: Low variable promoters had a weaker response to TNFα treatment than highly variable promoters.
source: In addition, low variable promoters had a weaker response (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Drug-target genes are regulated by highly variable promoters.
source: Furthermore, we observed drug-target genes and genes with GWAS hits to be regulated by highly variable promoters but essential genes to be regulated by low variable promoters (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Genes with GWAS hits are regulated by highly variable promoters.
source: Furthermore, we observed drug-target genes and genes with GWAS hits to be regulated by highly variable promoters but essential genes to be regulated by low variable promoters (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Essential genes are regulated by low variable promoters.
source: Furthermore, we observed drug-target genes and genes with GWAS hits to be regulated by highly variable promoters but essential genes to be regulated by low variable promoters (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Essential genes are associated with higher promoter expression.
source: Although essential genes are associated with higher promoter expression, this association is comparably weaker than that with promoter variability (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: The association between essential genes and promoter variability is stronger than the association with promoter expression.
source: Although essential genes are associated with higher promoter expression, this association is comparably weaker than that with promoter variability (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the strength of these associations.

claim: The variability observed in promoter activity across individuals is strongly associated with the regulation of its associated gene.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate the importance of low promoter variability for cell viability and survival in different conditions and reveal the responsiveness of highly variable promoters. They further indicate that the variability observed in promoter activity across individuals is strongly associated with the regulation of its associated gene, the expression breadth across cell types, and to some extent also the transcriptional noise across single cells, which reflects a selective trade-off between high stability and high responsiveness and specificity.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the functional analysis results.

claim: Promoter variability reflects a selective trade-off between high stability and high responsiveness and specificity.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate the importance of low promoter variability for cell viability and survival in different conditions and reveal the responsiveness of highly variable promoters. They further indicate that the variability observed in promoter activity across individuals is strongly associated with the regulation of its associated gene, the expression breadth across cell types, and to some extent also the transcriptional noise across single cells, which reflects a selective trade-off between high stability and high responsiveness and specificity.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: Highly variable promoters are enriched within narrow promoters having an interquartile range (IQR) of their CAGE-inferred TSSs within a width of 1–5 bp (p<2.2 × 10–16, OR = 2.04).
source: We observed an enrichment of highly variable promoters within narrow promoters having an interquartile range (IQR) of their CAGE-inferred TSSs within a width of 1–5 bp (p<2.2 × 10–16, OR = 2.04, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this enrichment with statistical test results.

claim: Low variable promoters are enriched among promoters with IQR size of 10–25 bp (p<2.2 × 10–16, OR = 1.44).
source: Low variable promoters, on the other hand, were enriched among those of size 10–25 bp (p<2.2 × 10–16, OR = 1.44, Fisher's exact test), but beyond this width the association is lost (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this enrichment with statistical test results.

claim: Low variable promoters are associated with a higher entropy than promoters with high variability.
source: We observed that low variable promoters are associated with a higher entropy than promoters with high variability (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Low variable promoters tend to have more TSSs substantially contributing to their overall expression across individuals.
source: Consistently, low variable promoters tend to have more TSSs substantially contributing to their overall expression across individuals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Higher entropy reflects an increased number of decomposed promoters, as indicated by their number of local maxima of CAGE signals.
source: Indeed, decomposition of multi-modal peaks within the CAGE TSS signals of promoters (Supplementary file 5) demonstrated that higher entropy reflects an increased number of decomposed promoters, as indicated by their number of local maxima of CAGE signals (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation from the decomposition analysis.

claim: Many decomposed promoters showed a vastly different variability across individuals compared to the promoters they originate from.
source: Interestingly, many of the decomposed promoters showed a vastly different variability across individuals compared to the promoters they originate from (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Low variable multi-modal promoters are associated with weakly or even negatively correlated pairs of decomposed promoters.
source: Indeed, we observed a strong association between promoter variability and the minimal expression correlation between decomposed promoter pairs within a promoter (Figure 4G). Low variable multi-modal promoters are associated with weakly or even negatively correlated pairs of decomposed promoters.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation from correlation analysis.

claim: Highly variable multi-modal promoters are associated with moderately or highly correlated pairs of decomposed promoters.
source: In contrast, highly variable multi-modal promoters are associated with moderately or highly correlated pairs of decomposed promoters.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Weak expression correlation between decomposed promoters of low variable promoters demonstrates that decomposed promoters may operate independently of each other.
source: The weak expression correlation between decomposed promoters of low variable promoters demonstrates that decomposed promoters may operate independently of each other, while negatively correlated pairs indicate a competition for the transcriptional machinery or a compensatory shift between decomposed promoters.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation of the correlation data.

claim: Negatively correlated pairs of decomposed promoters indicate a competition for the transcriptional machinery or a compensatory shift between decomposed promoters.
source: The weak expression correlation between decomposed promoters of low variable promoters demonstrates that decomposed promoters may operate independently of each other, while negatively correlated pairs indicate a competition for the transcriptional machinery or a compensatory shift between decomposed promoters.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: The association between decomposed promoter correlation and overall promoter stability was maintained when all decomposed promoter pairs were considered.
source: The association between decomposed promoter correlation and overall promoter stability was maintained when all decomposed promoter pairs were considered (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and could not be explained by CpG island status (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: The association between decomposed promoter correlation and overall promoter stability could not be explained by CpG island status.
source: The association between decomposed promoter correlation and overall promoter stability was maintained when all decomposed promoter pairs were considered (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and could not be explained by CpG island status (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Decomposed promoter expression correlation was associated with promoter width.
source: However, decomposed promoter expression correlation was associated with promoter width (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), demonstrating that complex low variable promoters with multiple decomposed promoters require larger promoter width, while broad promoter width does not necessarily lead to lower promoter variability.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Complex low variable promoters with multiple decomposed promoters require larger promoter width.
source: However, decomposed promoter expression correlation was associated with promoter width (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), demonstrating that complex low variable promoters with multiple decomposed promoters require larger promoter width, while broad promoter width does not necessarily lead to lower promoter variability.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: Broad promoter width does not necessarily lead to lower promoter variability.
source: However, decomposed promoter expression correlation was associated with promoter width (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), demonstrating that complex low variable promoters with multiple decomposed promoters require larger promoter width, while broad promoter width does not necessarily lead to lower promoter variability.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: Low variable promoters tend to have stronger +1 nucleosome positioning.
source: Indeed, comparison of +1 nucleosome positioning relative to the dominant TSS position of promoters across the panel revealed that low variable promoters tend to have stronger +1 nucleosome positioning (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation from nucleosome positioning analysis.

claim: Multi-modal low variable promoters with highly correlated decomposed promoters have strong +1 nucleosome positioning.
source: However, when analyzing specifically multi-modal low variable promoters (containing at least two decomposed promoters), a strong +1 nucleosome was only observed for promoters with highly correlated decomposed promoters (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Highly variable multi-modal promoters and those containing low correlated pairs of decomposed promoters exhibited more fuzzy +1 nucleosome positioning across cells.
source: Furthermore, highly variable multi-modal promoters and those containing low correlated pairs of decomposed promoters exhibited more fuzzy +1 nucleosome positioning across cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Low variable promoters with flexible TSS usage are characterized by less restrictive and more fuzzy +1 nucleosome positioning.
source: Our results thus demonstrate that low variable promoters with flexible TSS usage, that is, having weakly or negatively correlated decomposed promoters, are characterized by less restrictive and more fuzzy +1 nucleosome positioning.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the nucleosome positioning analysis.

claim: Flexible usage of core promoters within promoters with permissive nucleosomal architectures provide stability to the overall expression of a large subset of gene promoters with low variability.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that flexible usage of core promoters within promoters with permissive nucleosomal architectures provide stability to the overall expression of a large subset of gene promoters with low variability.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: 2,457 promoters were associated with at least one prQTL (5% FDR).
source: 2,457 promoters were associated with at least one prQTLs (5% FDR; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of promoters with prQTLs.

claim: prQTLs were more commonly associated with highly variable promoters.
source: While prQTLs were observed across all levels of promoter variability, they were more commonly associated with highly variable promoters (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: The effect size for the most significant prQTL variant for each promoter was positively associated with the expression variability of the promoter (Spearman's rank correlation ρ = 0.16, p< 2.2 × 10–16).
source: As expected, the effect size for the most significant prQTL variant (lead SNP) for each promoter was positively associated with the expression variability of the promoter (Spearman's rank correlation ρ = 0.16, p< 2.2 × 10–16, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this correlation with statistical test results.

claim: Low variable promoters are less likely to have prQTLs with large regulatory effects.
source: This indicates that, in addition to having fewer proximal genetic variants, low variable promoters are less likely to have prQTLs with large regulatory effects.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: QTLs of decomposed promoter expression (dprQTLs) exhibited similar prevalence across promoter variability classes.
source: However, QTLs of decomposed promoter expression (dprQTLs) exhibited similar prevalence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and maximum effect sizes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) across promoter variability classes.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: dprQTLs exhibited similar maximum effect sizes across promoter variability classes.
source: However, QTLs of decomposed promoter expression (dprQTLs) exhibited similar prevalence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and maximum effect sizes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) across promoter variability classes.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: A flexible TSS architecture can limit the impact of genetic variants on promoter expression.
source: This suggests that a flexible TSS architecture can limit the impact of genetic variants on promoter expression.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation based on the dprQTL analysis.

claim: 1,230 promoters were associated with at least one frQTL (5% FDR).
source: We identified 1,230 promoters to be associated with at least one frQTL (5% FDR; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of promoters with frQTLs.

claim: frQTLs were more commonly associated with decomposed promoters from low variable promoters.
source: Unlike the prQTLs and dprQTLs, the frQTLs were more commonly associated with decomposed promoters from low variable promoters (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: frQTLs associated with highly variable promoters tend to have a larger relative effect on the overall promoter activity compared to frQTLs associated with low variable promoters.
source: Although frQTLs were associated with promoters across the wide spectrum of promoter variabilities (Figure 5C), they showed a large difference in their relative effect on the overall promoter activity (maximal relative change in expression between reference and variant alleles; Figure 5F). frQTLs associated with highly variable promoters tend to have a larger relative effect on the overall promoter activity compared to frQTLs associated with low variable promoters.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: The association between frQTL relative effects and promoter variability is maintained at the gene level.
source: This association is further maintained at the gene level (adjusted RNA-seq Lappalainen et al., 2013 CV2; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 8), demonstrating that individual differences in decomposed promoter usage contribute to low promoter variability and, in turn, low gene variability.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation with citation.

claim: Individual differences in decomposed promoter usage contribute to low promoter variability and low gene variability.
source: This association is further maintained at the gene level (adjusted RNA-seq Lappalainen et al., 2013 CV2; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 8), demonstrating that individual differences in decomposed promoter usage contribute to low promoter variability and, in turn, low gene variability.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: 286 promoters of 284 genes were associated with stabilizing frQTLs, for which the same SNP was associated with at least two decomposed promoters with relative effects in opposite directions.
source: In total, we found 286 promoters (out of 1230) of 284 genes to be associated with stabilizing frQTLs, for which the same SNP was associated with at least two decomposed promoters (5% FDR) with relative effects in opposite directions (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding.

claim: TSS usage flexibility confers mutational robustness that stabilizes the variability of promoters and their associated genes.
source: Our results thus indicate that TSS usage flexibility confers mutational robustness that stabilizes the variability of promoters and their associated genes.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the frQTL analysis.

claim: Low variable promoters characterized by multiple decomposed promoters are less affected by the presence of genetic variants compared to highly variable promoters.
source: We demonstrate that low variable promoters characterized by multiple decomposed promoters (multi-modal TSS usage) are less affected by the presence of genetic variants compared to highly variable promoters.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: Plasticity in TSS usage provides a previously unreported mechanism of mutational robustness.
source: In addition, we find that part of this tolerance can be explained by a, previously unreported, mechanism of mutational robustness through plasticity in TSS usage.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this as a novel finding.

claim: The CNN model trained on DNA sequence alone (AUC = 0.84) performed better than the random forest classifier based on TF binding sites and CpG island status (AUC = 0.79).
source: Although the classifier based on TF binding site sequence and CpG island status was able to predict promoter variability well (AUC = 0.79 on the test set), it did not perform as well as the CNN model (AUC = 0.84 on the test set), which was trained on DNA sequence alone.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the performance of the two models.

claim: Additional information influencing variability may be encoded within the promoter sequence beyond TF binding sites and CpG content.
source: This indicates that additional information influencing variability may be encoded within the promoter sequence.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation based on the model comparison.

claim: The same features found to be predictive of low and high promoter variability across individuals, including CpG-content and TATA-boxes, are also associated with low and high transcriptional noise across individual cells.
source: Interestingly, the same features found to be predictive of low and high promoter variability across individuals, including CpG-content and TATA-boxes (TBP binding sites), are also associated with low and high transcriptional noise across individual cells (Faure et al., 2017; Morgan and Marioni, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation with citations to prior work.

claim: The presence of a TATA-box is associated with high gene expression variability in flies.
source: The presence of a TATA-box is also associated with high gene expression variability in flies (Sigalova et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this with citation to prior work.

claim: Some of the same underlying regulatory mechanisms that dictate low or high transcriptional noise across single cells are maintained and conserved between humans and flies at an individual level.
source: This suggests that some of the same underlying regulatory mechanisms that dictate low or high transcriptional noise across single cells are maintained and conserved between humans and flies at an individual level and manifested to control low and high expression variability across a population, respectively, as well as housekeeping or restricted activity across cell types.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: Low variable promoters are not strongly associated with broader width.
source: Despite a clear association with high promoter CpG content and housekeeping genes, low variable promoters were not strongly associated with a broader width, which we would expect from promoters in CpG islands and with housekeeping activity (Carninci et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation with citation.

claim: Low variability requires a certain minimum promoter width that can encompass a transcription initiation architecture competent of attenuating variability through flexible TSS usage.
source: Rather, our results suggest that low variability requires a certain minimum promoter width that can encompass a transcription initiation architecture competent of attenuating variability through flexible TSS usage.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: Switching between proximal clusters of TSSs within a larger promoter is fundamentally different from switching between alternative promoters.
source: Switching between proximal clusters of TSSs (decomposed promoters) within a larger promoter is fundamentally different from that between alternative promoters (Garieri et al., 2017; Valen et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2017), which will more likely lead to differences in transcript and protein isoforms.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this distinction with citations.

claim: A flexible initiation architecture enables several points of entries for RNA polymerase II to initiate in the same promoter.
source: Rather, a flexible initiation architecture enables several points of entries for RNA polymerase II to initiate in the same promoter.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this mechanism.

claim: Flexible TSS architecture ensures proper gene expression across different cell types and developmental stages.
source: This ensures proper gene expression across different cell types (FANTOM Consortium and the RIKEN PMI and CLST (DGT) et al., 2014; Kawaji et al., 2006) and developmental stages (Haberle et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this with citations to prior work.

claim: ETS factors can interact with transcriptional co-activators and chromatin modifying complexes.
source: Interestingly, ETS factors, here associated with low variable promoters, can interact with transcriptional co-activators and chromatin modifying complexes (Curina et al., 2017; Göös et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this with citations.

claim: ETS factors may play a role in TSS selection in promoters with multi-modal architectures.
source: ETS factors may therefore play a role in TSS selection in promoters with multi-modal architectures (Lam et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly suggests this mechanism with citation.

claim: Flexibility in TSS usage within a promoter is associated with low variability across individuals for the same cell type.
source: Here, we show that such flexibility is also associated with low variability across individuals for the same cell type.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding.

claim: Plasticity in TSS usage within a promoter confers a previously unreported layer of mutational robustness that can buffer the effects of genetic variants.
source: Our findings further indicate that plasticity in TSS usage within a promoter confers a, previously unreported, layer of mutational robustness that can buffer the effects of genetic variants, leading to limited or no impact on the overall promoter expression.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this as a novel finding.

claim: The presence of weak or negatively correlated expression patterns between decomposed promoters for a large number of promoters suggests that buffering events will be revealed for more genes with an increased sample size.
source: Of note, the presence of weak or negatively correlated expression patterns between decomposed promoters for a large number of promoters suggests that such buffering events will be revealed for more genes with an increased sample size.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this speculation.

claim: Flexibility in TSS usage may ensure transcriptional robustness of genes both in different environments and in the face of genetic variation.
source: Flexibility in TSS usage may ensure transcriptional robustness of genes both in different environments and in the face of genetic variation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: Promoter shape is generally conserved across orthologous promoters.
source: Since promoter shape is generally conserved across orthologous promoters (Carninci et al., 2006; Hoskins et al., 2011), it is plausible that robustness through flexible TSS usage is a conserved mechanism.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this with citations to prior work.

claim: Robustness through flexible TSS usage is plausibly a conserved mechanism.
source: Since promoter shape is generally conserved across orthologous promoters (Carninci et al., 2006; Hoskins et al., 2011), it is plausible that robustness through flexible TSS usage is a conserved mechanism.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this speculation based on conservation of promoter shape.

claim: Genetic variants may affect promoter shape for ubiquitously expressed genes in flies with limited effect on promoter expression.
source: In support, genetic variants may affect promoter shape for ubiquitously expressed genes in flies with limited effect on promoter expression (Schor et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this with citation to prior work in flies.

claim: Changes in promoter shape in flies likely recapitulate the plasticity in TSS usage across human LCLs.
source: Changes in promoter shape in flies thus likely recapitulates the plasticity in TSS usage across human LCLs, despite apparent differences in core promoter elements, promoter nucleotide content, and regulatory features between flies and humans.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: Variability in promoter activity across individuals partly reflects the stochasticity in gene expression across cells.
source: This suggests that variability in promoter activity across individuals partly reflects the stochasticity in gene expression across cells.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: Mechanisms that contribute to the buffering of stochastic noise at a single cell level can also contribute to the attenuation of genetic and environmental variation at an individual level.
source: Given that the underlying sources of variation are different, for example, genetic and environmental versus stochastic, this indicates that mechanisms that contribute to the buffering of stochastic noise at a single cell level can also contribute to the attenuation of genetic and environmental variation at an individual level.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: Low variable promoters with flexible TSS usage are associated with fuzzy +1 nucleosome positioning across cells within an individual.
source: Notably, these promoters are also associated with a fuzzy +1 nucleosome positioning across cells within an individual.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Positional shifts of nucleosomes in coordination with shifts in core promoter usage may be due to an inherent property of low variable promoters in addition to the influence by genetic variation.
source: This indicates that positional shifts of nucleosomes in coordination with shifts in core promoter usage may be due to an inherent property of these promoters in addition to the influence by genetic variation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: Multiple configurations of accessible chromatin may exist for low variable promoters across single cells, which may cause stochastic TSS selection with no or only low impact on expression level.
source: Our observations indicate that multiple configurations of accessible chromatin may exist for low variable promoters across single cells, which may cause stochastic TSS selection with no or only low impact on expression level.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: A high density of pyrimidine/purine (YR) dinucleotides within broad promoters provides flexibility for transcription initiation sites in the absence of strong positional signals like the TATA box.
source: This is compatible with a high density of pyrimidine/purine (YR) dinucleotides within broad promoters (Carninci et al., 2006; Frith et al., 2007), which provide a flexibility for transcription initiation sites in the absence of strong positional signals like the TATA box (Carninci et al., 2006; FANTOM Consortium and the RIKEN PMI and CLST (DGT) et al., 2014; Müller and Tora, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this with citations to prior work.

claim: Genetic variants biasing TSS selection and the preference for any open chromatin configuration may cause observable shifts in TSS usage between individuals, enabled by the flexible nucleosome and TSS architecture of the promoter.
source: Genetic variants biasing such TSS selection and the preference for any open chromatin configuration may therefore cause observable shifts in TSS usage between individuals, enabled by the flexible nucleosome and TSS architecture of the promoter.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: The regulatory programs of EBV-immortalized LCLs are susceptible to genotype-independent sources of variation, such as primary cellular heterogeneity and EBV's viral cellular reprogramming.
source: It is important to note that the regulatory programs of EBV-immortalized LCLs, like other cultured cells, have been shown to be susceptible to genotype-independent sources of variation, such as primary cellular heterogeneity and EBV's viral cellular reprogramming (Choy et al., 2008; Ozgyin et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this limitation with citations.

claim: Non-genetic variation would rather dampen than elevate the associations and effect sizes reported in the study.
source: While we cannot exclude that such sources may influence the measured variability of some genes, we speculate that non-genetic variation would rather dampen than elevate the associations and effect sizes we report here, in particular the decomposed promoter switches highlighted by our genotype association analysis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this speculation.

claim: The regulation of transcriptional noise across single cells reflects specificity across cell types and dispersion across individuals with shared mechanisms conferring stochastic, genetic and environmental robustness.
source: Taken together, our results favor a model in which the regulation of transcriptional noise across single cells reflects specificity across cell types and dispersion across individuals with shared mechanisms conferring stochastic, genetic and environmental robustness (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this model.

claim: Regulatory mechanisms that ensure broad expression across cell types may enforce low variability across individuals and single cells.
source: First, the link between low transcriptional noise and low individual variability of promoters and their associations with ubiquitous and essential genes indicates that regulatory mechanisms that ensure broad expression across cell types may enforce low variability across individuals and single cells.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this implication of the model.

claim: Encoding responsiveness or developmentally restricted expression patterns of gene promoters may require high stochasticity in expression across single cells, which in turn may disallow ubiquitous expression across cell types.
source: Second, our results indicate that encoding responsiveness or developmentally restricted expression patterns of gene promoters may require high stochasticity in expression across single cells, which in turn may disallow ubiquitous expression across cell types.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this implication.

claim: Increased variability is not just reflecting the absence of regulatory mechanisms that attenuate variability but the presence of those that amplify it.
source: Thus, it is likely that increased variability is not just reflecting the absence of regulatory mechanisms that attenuate variability but the presence of those that amplify it.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: Cell-type restricted, responsive and developmental genes may be more susceptible to trait-associated genetic variants.
source: Finally, given that mutational robustness through flexible TSS usage is mostly associated with low variable genes, this implies that cell-type restricted, responsive and developmental genes may be more susceptible to trait-associated genetic variants, which finds support in the literature (Finucane et al., 2015; Roadmap Epigenomics Consortium et al., 2015; Timshel et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this implication with citations to supporting literature.
